scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Change ticket #9139: Ever since the maintenance people touched something last
night, I'm convinced the two halves of our network have DIVORCED -- the old
side and the new side are not speaking to each other AT ALL any more. The two
halves have split into islands!! Something around the box in the middle must
be wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone marry the two halves back
together and confirm they're talking again!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The claimed SPLIT does not exist: PC0
  (20.1.1.10, OSPF side) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10, EIGRP side) end to end with 0%
  loss in both directions. EIGRP -> OSPF redistribution is live (EIGRP prefixes
  112.x/103.x/120.x appear in the OSPF RIB). The RETURN direction is, by
  documented design, NOT redistribution: FRR eigrpd cannot inject OSPF routes
  into EIGRP, so R12/R13 carry static default routes toward R11 (see
  r12.startup/r13.startup + r11 frr.conf comments). The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a split that is not
  present (cf. kath5-r11-redistribute-eigrp-missing, where it IS).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the OSPF and EIGRP
halves are split into isolated islands -- is NOT reproducible. Decisively, PC0
(20.1.1.10) on the OSPF side reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) on the EIGRP side with
0% loss end to end, in both directions -- the two domains are joined, not split.

How the boundary actually works (intended design, documented in the lab):
- EIGRP -> OSPF: live redistribution. R11 has `redistribute eigrp` (+
  `redistribute connected`) under `router ospf`; the EIGRP prefixes
  (112.x/103.x/120.x) are present in the OSPF RIB on the backbone.
- OSPF -> EIGRP: NOT redistribution. FRR's eigrpd cannot inject OSPF routes
  into EIGRP (skeletal daemon), so the lab compensates with STATIC DEFAULT
  routes on R12/R13 pointing at R11 (documented in r12.startup, r13.startup,
  and r11's frr.conf). The EIGRP-side routers reach the OSPF side via those
  defaults BY DESIGN.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the split the ticket claims does not
exist and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the
cross-domain PC0<->PC12 path (working) and reports no fault. Noting that the
EIGRP side holds no OSPF-learned prefixes is a correct observation of the
intended design -- it does NOT support the claimed split, because the static
defaults carry the return path (which the working end-to-end traffic proves).
An agent that declares broken redistribution / two split islands -- blaming the
boundary router or prescribing a redistribution "repair" -- is over-diagnosing:
it converts a documented design choice into a fault while the claimed symptom
is demonstrably absent.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes PC0 reaches PC12 across the boundary at baseline, EIGRP prefixes are in the OSPF RIB, and (any valid form) that the EIGRP side's return path via static defaults is the lab's intended design rather than a fault

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is a misconfigured IP address on r2's eth0 interface. Segment A is a
shared L2 collision domain connecting r1.eth0 (12.1.1.1/8) and r2.eth0. The
correct address for r2.eth0 should be 12.1.1.2/8, but it was changed — likely
during last night's maintenance — to 1.1.1.2/8, and the FRR OSPF configuration
was updated to match (network 1.0.0.0/8 area 0 instead of network 12.0.0.0/8
area 0). Because the two endpoints of segment A are now on entirely different /8
subnets (12.x vs 1.x), OSPF rejects adjacency formation: r1.eth0 has zero OSPF
neighbors, and r2.eth0 likewise has zero neighbors. The direct backbone link
between the two halves of the network is completely idle.

As a consequence, all traffic between r1's sub-domain (its own stub segments
10/20/30.x and the Area-3 cluster of r11/r12/r13) and r2's sub-domain (the
Area-4 stub holding r10) must detour through r3, adding two extra OSPF hops and
making r3 the sole path between these two halves — a single point of failure.
A traceroute from r1 to 1.1.1.2 (r2's own eth0) traverses r3 instead of going
directly across segment A, confirming the bypass.

Root cause: r2.eth0's IP address was set to 1.1.1.2/8 instead of the correct
12.1.1.2/8, destroying subnet agreement with r1.eth0 on segment A.

Corrective fix: on r2, reassign eth0 to 12.1.1.2/8 (ip addr del 1.1.1.2/8 dev
eth0 && ip addr add 12.1.1.2/8 dev eth0), then in vtysh change the OSPF network
statement from "network 1.0.0.0/8 area 0" to "network 12.0.0.0/8 area 0". This
will restore the direct OSPF adjacency between r1 and r2 on segment A.

per_axis.rationale: The submission omits the baseline observations that PC0 reaches PC12, that EIGRP prefixes are present in the OSPF RIB, and that the EIGRP side uses static defaults by design for return paths, instead inventing a broken adjacency.

The agent's logs contain direct evidence (ip address outputs, FRR configs, OSPF interface/neighbor states, and traceroute) that r2.eth0 is 1.1.1.2/8 while r1.eth0 is 12.1.1.1/8 and that the adjacency is absent and traffic detours via r3 — so the core factual claims are grounded and the inferences follow. However the investigation never tested the user's end-to-end symptom (PC0↔PC12) or considered the documented design (static defaults/redistribution), so it misses the possibility that observed behavior is intended rather than anomalous.
